profile_name: Interrogation Documentary — 'Has No Idea' Irony, Real Footage Carries the Story
based_on: The leading faceless English channel of 2026 in police-footage documentaries (~7,700 words including interrogation dialogue, 40–75 minutes, human narrator). No names, places or cases from the original are kept.
best_for: ONLY when real interrogation, bodycam or 911 recordings of the case are publicly available and lawfully sourced. Without footage, use another style.

secondary: lightly ironic about the suspect's confidence
never: inventing what is not on tape

point_of_view.narration: third-person, present tense around the footage ('Right now, she's being questioned…'), past tense for background
point_of_view.viewer_address: 'What you're about to watch is…' framing; comment questions at the end

audience_addressing_style: narrator as a guide who knows the ending and lets the viewer watch the suspect not know it

hook_style.type: cold open on a real line from the interrogation, then the irony stated plainly
hook_style.formula: [2–4 real lines from the interview]. This is [name], [job, years]. Right now, [he/she] is being questioned about [crime] from [N] years ago. [He/She] is the one who did it. [He/She] just doesn't know that investigators already know it, too. [One more real line]. What you're about to watch is how [investigators] got [the suspect] to [walk into the truth] using nothing but a conversation.
hook_style.length_words: 150–250 of narration around the quoted lines

narrative_structure.type: interrogation cold open → crime day reconstruction → original investigation and wrong theory → the evidence that waited → how investigators set up the interview → long interrogation segments with narrator bridges → arrest → trial and sentence → later admissions → comment questions
beats_in_order: 1. Interrogation cold open and irony line.
2. Date and place; the day of the crime reconstructed minute by minute.
3. The scene that looked like something else (a burglary, an accident).
4. Years of the wrong theory; the evidence that sat in storage.
5. The new test and the shock of whom it pointed to.
6. Covert evidence collection (a discarded cup or straw).
7. The interview strategy explained before the footage.
8. Footage blocks of 1–3 minutes, each introduced and then explained ('Notice what she does here…').
9. The moment the suspect realises; the arrest outside the room.
10. Trial, sentence, parole hearings, later admissions.
11. Two direct questions to the audience for the comments.

pacing.overall: alternates fast narrated reconstruction with slow real-time footage
pacing.footage_rule: never more than ~2–3 minutes of uninterrupted footage before the narrator adds context or analysis

sentence_style.mix: short ironic statements, procedural explanations, analysis of body language and word choice
sentence_style.questions: only in the final comment prompt and in quoted dialogue

language_style.register: plain, slightly wry documentary English; interview-technique vocabulary explained

characters.victim: remembered at the start and at the sentence

dialogue.use: real recorded dialogue is the backbone (40%+ of runtime)

humor: dry irony only, never at the victim's expense

emotional_tone.arc: dramatic irony → curiosity → tension → release at the arrest → sober justice

common_devices: 'What you're about to watch is how…' promise
narrator pointing out tells in the footage

call_to_action_style.closing: 'So, what stands out to you most about this case? Is it [A]? Or that [B]? Let us know what you think in the comments.'

visual_cue_prompts.footage: real interrogation or bodycam in a framed player with source caption, subtitles, names on first appearance
visual_cue_prompts.reconstruction: maps, photos, silhouettes replacing bodies in scene photos
visual_cue_prompts.evidence: the decisive object close-up, lab graphic

safety_and_compliance: Footage must be lawfully obtained (public records, official releases); credit the source on screen and in the description.
Add substantial narration and analysis around every footage block (reused-content policy).
Blur minors, bystanders and graphic scene photos.
Never put a bodycam or CCTV frame on stock footage to make it look like real case footage.

script_formatting_rules.parts: The final script must be sectioned into 10 parts, each part at least 800 words (narration only; footage segments are planned separately).
script_formatting_rules.total_length: The full narration must be 8,000+ words in total.
script_formatting_rules.no_headings: No section headings, no part numbers, no titles inside the text.
script_formatting_rules.no_line_breaks: No line breaks: the whole script is one continuous block of text.
script_formatting_rules.no_symbols: No underscores, no bullet points, no brackets, no stage directions, no visual cues, no comments.
script_formatting_rules.no_wrappers: No introductory statement and no closing statement outside the narration itself.
script_formatting_rules.delivery: Send the whole script in one batch, only the script text, with nothing before or after it.
